references.text: Isaiah prophesied about the Messiah as the suffering servant: "He was despised, forsaken by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief." This points directly to Jesus' words that the Son of Man must first suffer greatly and be rejected. See [ref:Jes 53:3|Isaiah 53:3].

"The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone." This psalm about rejection and vindication is a central theme that Jesus connects to his own suffering and rejection by this generation. See [ref:Sal 118:22|Psalm 118:22].

Jesus predicts his suffering for the first time: The Son of Man must suffer greatly and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes. The parallel to Luke 17:25 is clear with the words "πολλὰ παθεῖν καὶ ἀποδοκιμασθῆναι". See [ref:Mark 8:31|Mark 8:31].

Luke's own parallel to Mark's first prediction of suffering, where Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer greatly and be rejected. The same wording as in [ref:Luk 17:25|Luke 17:25]. See [ref:Luk 9:22|Luke 9:22].

The second prediction of suffering in Luke: "The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men." This emphasizes the necessity of Jesus' suffering before his glorification. See [ref:Luk 9:44|Luke 9:44].

The third prediction of suffering in Luke, where Jesus describes in detail his coming suffering, mockery, and death in Jerusalem. Again it is emphasized that the Son of Man must first suffer. See [ref:Luk 18:31-33|Luke 18:31-33].

Matthew's version of the first prediction of suffering, where Jesus explains that he must suffer greatly at the hands of the elders, chief priests, and scribes, be killed, and rise on the third day. See [ref:Matt 16:21|Matthew 16:21].

Peter explains that God had beforehand declared through the prophets that his Messiah would suffer. God's plan required (δεῖ) that Christ must first suffer, just as Jesus himself said. See [ref:Apg 3:18|Acts 3:18].

Peter describes Christ as "the living stone which was rejected by men, but is chosen and precious to God." The rejection of Christ by "this generation" is fulfilled here. See [ref:1 Pet 2:4|1 Peter 2:4].

The risen Jesus asks the Emmaus travelers: "Was it not necessary for the Messiah to suffer these things and then enter into his glory?" Here the necessity (δεῖ/ἔδει) of suffering before glory is confirmed, an identical theme as in [ref:Luk 17:25|Luke 17:25]. See [ref:Luk 24:26|Luke 24:26].

Isaiah's description of the suffering servant who was afflicted and mistreated, taken away by oppression and judgment, points to Jesus' suffering and rejection as a divine necessity. See [ref:Jes 53:7-8|Isaiah 53:7-8].
